screens.heading: Rights and responsibilities
screens.body: The officer will ask what citizens can do and must do — questions like:
screens.afterQuote: The test asks about rights and duties as two short lists. This lesson gives you both — and the difference between them.
screens.coverageLine: It covers 10 of the 128 on the test.
screens.afterTest: And this lesson is different from every other one: it is about you. These are the rights you will hold and the promises you will make.

screens.question: Which of these belongs to everyone living in America — citizen or not?
screens.feedback: Freedom of speech belongs to everyone here. Voting belongs to citizens. That line — everyone vs. citizens — is the key to this whole lesson.

bodyList: Joining any organization changes your standing.
A guest at a community center is welcome and safe — but members vote at the meetings, and members pay the dues.
Belonging brings both: a louder voice, and real duties.
bodyList2: Living in America already gives you strong protections.
screens.closing: Becoming a citizen adds the member's voice — and the member's promises.

cards.def: a freedom the law protects for you.
cards.example: The right to vote belongs to citizens.

cards.def: a duty — something you must or should do.
a group of citizens who decide a court case.

cards.example: At your ceremony you will take an oath.
The oath asks for loyalty to the United States.

paragraphs: Remember the Bill of Rights from the rulebook lesson — protections for people living in the United States, not only citizens.

Everyone here holds these: freedom of speech, freedom of expression, freedom of assembly (gathering in groups), freedom to petition the government (asking it to change something), freedom of religion, and the right to bear arms. These protect you today, before your ceremony.

Citizens hold three more, and they are the ones that steer the country: vote in federal elections, run for federal office, and serve on a jury. Notice what all three share — they are ways of having a say in how the country is run, not just living in it. Jury service is also a responsibility — it is both a right you hold and a duty you may be called to perform.

Voting itself was widened by four amendments — remember, changes to the rulebook: any race can vote, women and men can vote, no poll tax (you cannot be charged money to vote), and citizens eighteen and older can vote.
screens.resolution: The full story of that widening is Lesson 7.
screens.handle: Everyone here holds rights. Citizens hold the vote.

paragraphs: Everyone who earns money here pays federal taxes — required by law, and it is how the country pays for what it does. Men aged 18 through 25 register for the Selective Service — a list, required by law, that makes a draft fair if one is ever needed.

And at your ceremony, you will stand and take the Oath of Allegiance — the member's promises: give up loyalty to other countries, defend the Constitution, obey the laws of the United States, serve the nation if needed, be loyal to the United States.
On the test, this is Question 67. In your life, it is the moment you become a citizen. It is the only test answer you will one day say out loud, with your hand raised, at your own ceremony.

How do people become citizens at all? Three doors: born in the United States (a promise written in the 14th Amendment — its story is in Lesson 7), naturalize — your door, the one this course walks you to — or derive citizenship through parents.
screens.handle: Rights and responsibilities are two halves of one standing.
screens.alt: A polling place: a Vote Here sign beside open voting booths, with people filling in ballots.

screens.heading: Rights protect you now. The member's voice comes at the ceremony.
screens.example: A permanent resident writes a letter to a newspaper criticizing a law — fully protected, citizen or not. The same person cannot yet vote on that law.
screens.nonExample: 'Rights are things I get; responsibilities are optional.' No — they are two halves of one standing. The same oath that gives you the ballot asks for your loyalty.
screens.takeaway: Rights: yes, today. The member's voice: at the ceremony.

screens.heading: Two words on the test sound alike. Do not mix them up.

termA.name: A right
termA.def: something the law protects for you — speech, religion, assembly.

termB.name: A responsibility
termB.def: something the law or the community expects from you — taxes, jury service.

screens.resolution: Voting is special — it is a right you hold and a responsibility worth exercising.

items.instructions: Tap to sort each one into Everyone here or Citizens only.

items.question: What is one way Americans can serve their country? Many answers are accepted — pick one of them.
Why do men aged 18–25 register for Selective Service when there is no draft?
options: So that a draft, if ever needed, would be fair
Because they must join the military
Because it is required to vote

items.question: The officer asks this. The question tells you the count — what should you do?
items.cardText: Name two promises that new citizens make in the Oath of Allegiance.
options: Give two, then stop — extra answers only add chances for mistakes
Give as many as you can remember
Give one, because any one is enough
